$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & =\int v(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int {csc}^{2}⁡(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =-\operatorname{cot}⁡(t)+C\end{aligned}

$$

Therefore, the position $x$ of the particle at time $t$ is 

$$
x(t)=-\operatorname{cot}⁡(t)+1.
$$

questions.problem: A particle moves along a straight line relative to a fixed origin $O$ with velocity $v(t)=3{t}^{2}+2t,$ where $t$ is the time. If the particle is at the position $x=15$ when $t=2,$ calculate the position $x$ of the particle at time $t>0.$
questions.worked_solution:
We start by integrating the velocity to get $x(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & =\int v(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int (3{t}^{2}+2t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={t}^{3}+{t}^{2}+C\end{aligned}
$$

To determine $C,$ we use the fact that $x(2)=15.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}15 & =(2)^{3}+(2)^{2}+C \\ 15 & =8+4+C \\ C & =3.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the position $x$ of the particle at time $t$ is 

$$
x(t)={t}^{3}+{t}^{2}+3.
$$

questions.problem: A particle moves along a straight line relative to a fixed origin $O$ with velocity $v(t)=4{t}^{3}+{t}^{2}+6t,$ where $t$ is the time. If the particle is at the position $x=11$ when $t=1,$ calculate the position $x$ of the particle at time $t>0.$
questions.worked_solution:
We start by integrating the velocity to get $x(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & =\int v(t)\,dt \\  & =\int (4{t}^{3}+{t}^{2}+6t)dt \\  & ={t}^{4}+\frac{{t}^{3}}{3}+3{t}^{2}+C\end{aligned}
$$

To determine $C,$ we use the fact that $x(1)=11.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}11 & =(1)^{4}+\frac{(1)^{3}}{3}+3(1)^{2}+C \\ 11 & =1+\frac{1}{3}+3+C \\ C & =\frac{20}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the position $x$ of the particle at time $t$ is 

$$
x(t)={t}^{4}+\frac{{t}^{3}}{3}+3{t}^{2}+\frac{20}{3}.
$$

questions.problem: A particle moves along a straight line relative to a fixed origin $O$ with velocity $v(t)=\frac{1}{4}t-{t}^{2},$ where $t>0$ is the time. If the particle is at the position $x=-7$ when $t=3,$ calculate the position $x$ of the particle at time $t.$
questions.worked_solution:
We start by integrating the velocity to get $x(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & =\int v(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int (\frac{1}{4}t-{t}^{2})\text{d}t \\  & =\frac{1}{8}{t}^{2}-\frac{1}{3}{t}^{3}+C\end{aligned}
$$

To determine $C,$ we use the fact that $x(3)=-7.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}-7 & =\frac{1}{8}(3)^{2}-\frac{1}{3}(3)^{3}+C \\ -7 & =-\frac{63}{8}+C \\ C & =\frac{7}{8}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the position $x$ of the particle at time $t$ is 

$$
x(t)=\frac{1}{8}{t}^{2}-\frac{1}{3}{t}^{3}+\frac{7}{8}.
$$

A particle moves along a straight line relative to a fixed origin $O$ with acceleration $a(t)={e}^{3t},$ where $t\ge 0$ is the time. If the particle has position $x=0$ and velocity $v=1$ when $t=0,$ the position $x$ of the particle at time $t$ is

$x(t)=$
{{field-1}}.
questions.worked_solution:
We start by integrating the acceleration to get the velocity $v(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\int a(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int {e}^{3t}\,\text{d}t \\  & =\frac{1}{3}{e}^{3t}+C\end{aligned}
$$

To determine $C,$ we use the fact that $v(0)=1.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}1 & =\frac{1}{3}{e}^{0}+C \\ 1 & =\frac{1}{3}+C \\ C & =\frac{2}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

So the velocity is given by $v(t)=\frac{1}{3}{e}^{3t}+\frac{2}{3}.$

Now, we integrate the velocity to get $x(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & =\int v(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int (\frac{1}{3}{e}^{3t}+\frac{2}{3})\,\text{d}t \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\int {e}^{3t}\,\text{d}t+\frac{2}{3}\int \,\text{d}t \\  & =\frac{1}{9}{e}^{3t}+\frac{2}{3}t+K\end{aligned}
$$

To determine $K$, we use the fact that $x(0)=0.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}0 & =\frac{1}{9}{e}^{0}+\frac{2}{3}(0)+K \\ 0 & =\frac{1}{9}+K \\ K & =-\frac{1}{9}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the position $x$ of the particle at time $t$ is 

$$
x(t)=\frac{1}{9}{e}^{3t}+\frac{2}{3}t-\frac{1}{9}.
$$

questions.problem: A particle moves along a straight line relative to a fixed origin $O$ with acceleration $a(t)=3\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t),$ where $t\ge 0$ is the time. If the particle has position $x=5$ and velocity $v=1$ when $t=0,$ calculate the position $x$ of the particle at time $t.$
questions.worked_solution:
We start by integrating the acceleration to get the velocity $v(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\int a(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int 3\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)\text{d}t \\  & =-\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)+C\end{aligned}
$$

To determine $C,$ we use the fact that $v(0)=1.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}1 & =-\operatorname{cos}⁡(3(0))+C \\ 1 & =-1+C \\ C & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

So the velocity is given by $v(t)=2-\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t).$

Now, we integrate the velocity to get $x(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & =\int v(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int (2-\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t))\text{d}t \\  & =2t-\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)+K\end{aligned}
$$

To determine $K,$ we use the fact that $x(0)=5.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}5 & =2(0)-\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3(0))+K \\ K & =5.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the position $x$ of the particle at time $t$ is 

$$
x(t)=2t-\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)+5.
$$

questions.problem: A particle moves along a straight line relative to a fixed origin $O$ with acceleration $a(t)=1-6t,$ where $t\ge 0$ is the time. If the particle has position $x=2$ and velocity $v=4$ when $t=0,$ calculate the position $x$ of the particle at time $t>0.$
questions.worked_solution:
We start by integrating the acceleration to get the velocity $v(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\int a(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int (1-6t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =t-3{t}^{2}+C\end{aligned}
$$

To determine $C,$ we use the fact that $v(0)=4.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}4 & =(0)-3(0)^{2}+C \\ C & =4.\end{aligned}
$$

So the velocity is given by $v(t)=t-3{t}^{2}+4.$

Now, we integrate the velocity to get $x(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & =\int v(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int (t-3{t}^{2}+4)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{t}^{2}-{t}^{3}+4t+K\end{aligned}
$$

To determine $K,$ we use the fact that $x(0)=2.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}2 & =\frac{1}{2}(0)^{2}-(0)^{3}+4(0)+K \\ K & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the position $x$ of the particle at time $t$ is 

$$
x(t)=\frac{1}{2}{t}^{2}-{t}^{3}+4t+2.
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\int a(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int (20{t}^{3}+12)\,\text{d}t \\  & =5{t}^{4}+12t+C\end{aligned}
$$

To determine $C,$ we use the fact that $v(0)=1.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}1 & =0+0+C \\ C & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

So the velocity is given by $v(t)=5{t}^{4}+12t+1.$

Now, we integrate the velocity to get $x(t):$

$$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}-3 & =0+0+0+K \\ K & =-3.\end{aligned}

Therefore, the position $x$ of the particle at time $t$ is 

$$

questions.problem: A particle moves along a straight line relative to a fixed origin $O$ with acceleration $a(t)=2\operatorname{cos}⁡(t),$ where $t\ge 0$ is the time. If the particle has position $x=2\pi $ and velocity $v=4$ when $t=\frac{\pi }{2},$ calculate the position $x$ of the particle at time $t.$
questions.worked_solution:
We start by integrating the acceleration to get the velocity $v(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\int a(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int 2\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)\text{d}t \\  & =2\operatorname{sin}⁡(t)+C\end{aligned}
$$

To determine $C,$ we use the fact that $v(\frac{\pi }{2})=4.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}4 & =2\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})+C \\ 4 & =2(1)+C \\ C & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

So the velocity is given by $v(t)=2\operatorname{sin}⁡(t)+2.$

Now, we integrate the velocity to get $x(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & =\int v(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int (2\operatorname{sin}⁡(t)+2)\text{d}t \\  & =-2\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)+2t+K\end{aligned}
$$

To determine $K,$ we use the fact that $x(\frac{\pi }{2})=2\pi .$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}2\pi  & =-2\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})+2(\frac{\pi }{2})+K \\ 2\pi  & =-2(0)+\pi +K \\ K & =\pi .\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the position $x$ of the particle at time $t$ is 

$$
x(t)=-2\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)+2t+\pi .
$$

canonical_examples.problem: A particle moves along a straight line relative to a fixed origin $O$ with velocity $v(t) = 2t+3t^2,$ where $t\geq 0$ is the time. If the particle is at the position $x=1$ when $t=0,$ calculate the position $x$ of the particle at time $t.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
We start by integrating the velocity to get $x(t)\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & =\int v(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int (2t+3{t}^{2})\,\text{d}t \\  & ={t}^{2}+{t}^{3}+C\end{aligned}
$$

To determine $C,$ we use the fact that $x(0) = 1.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}1 & =(0)^{2}+(0)^{3}+C \\ C & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the position $x$ of the particle at time $t$ is

$$
x(t) = t^3+t^2+1.
$$

canonical_examples.problem: A particle moves along a straight line relative to a fixed origin $O$ with acceleration $a(t) = 1-2t,$ where $t\geq 0$ is the time. If the particle has position $x=1$ and velocity $v=2$ when $t=1,$ calculate the position $x$ of the particle at time $t >0.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
We start by integrating the acceleration to get the velocity $v(t)\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\int a(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int (1-2t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =t-{t}^{2}+C\end{aligned}
$$

To determine $C,$ we use the fact that $v(1) = 2.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}2 & =(1)-(1)^{2}+C \\ C & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

So the velocity is given by $v(t) = t-t^2 + 2.$

Now, we integrate the velocity to get $x(t)\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & =\int v(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int (t-{t}^{2}+2)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{t}^{2}-\frac{1}{3}{t}^{3}+2t+K\end{aligned}
$$

To determine $K,$ we use the fact that $x(1) = 1.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}1 & =\frac{1}{2}(1)^{2}-\frac{1}{3}(1)^{3}+2(1)+K \\ K & =-\frac{7}{6}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the position $x$ of the particle at time $t$ is 

$$
x(t) = \dfrac{1}{2}t^2-\dfrac{1}{3}t^3 +2t -\dfrac{7}{6}.
$$
